Cross-Platform System Call Analysis, Kernel Architecture Comparison, and Parallel Kalman Filter Computation
Comprehensive Empirical Study on Linux (POSIX) and Microsoft Windows (Windows NT)

Course: CT-353 Operating Systems CLO 1 (C2): Describe the concepts, structure and design of operating systems. CLO 2 (C4): Analyze operating system design and its impact on application design and performance. Complex Problem Solving Attributes: CP-2 (Depth of Analysis), CP-8 (Interdependence), CP-9 (Requirements Identification) Team Members: [Group of 3 Students] | Submission Date: Fall Term 2026

Operating systems represent the quintessential abstraction bridge between computer microarchitecture and user applications. The strict separation between unprivileged User Mode (Ring 3) and privileged Kernel Mode (Ring 0) ensures process isolation, address space protection, and hardware stability. Mediating every single interaction across this security boundary are System Calls.

In this Complex Computing Problem (CCP), our team designed and implemented an end-to-end, cross-platform systems software suite in modern C++ (C++17). The project explores the core operating system mechanisms across two distinct architectural paradigms: the Linux monolithic POSIX kernel and the Windows NT hybrid executive kernel.

The project addresses three fundamental deliverables: (1) implementing and functionally testing 15 essential system calls spanning File I/O, Process Lifecycle, Virtual Memory, Inter-Process Communication (IPC), and File Security; (2) empirically benchmarking their microsecond-level invocation latency and resource overhead; and (3) integrating these low-level system calls into a multi-process, memory-mapped Kinematic Kalman Filter for real-time sensor trajectory estimation.

3.1 Privilege Rings and Hardware Traps (Ring 3 to Ring 0)
When an application requires operating system services, it cannot execute privileged CPU instructions directly. Instead, modern x86_64 processors execute the hardware SYSCALL instruction:
1. CPU Privilege Switch: The processor transitions from Current Privilege Level (CPL) 3 to CPL 0 (Kernel Mode).
2. Stack Pointer Switch: The CPU switches the stack pointer %rsp from the user stack to the per-thread kernel task stack.
3. Register Context Preservation: User-space instruction pointer (%rip) and flags (%rflags) are saved into %rcx and %r11.
4. Vector Dispatching: The CPU vectors to the System Call Handler address previously registered in the Model Specific Register (MSR_LSTAR).
3.2 Linux sys_call_table vs. Windows NT SSDT

In Linux, the kernel inspects the %rax register as an index into the global sys_call_table array. Parameters are passed according to System V AMD64 ABI (%rdi, %rsi, %rdx, %r10, %r8, %r9). Upon completion, SYSRETQ restores user-space execution.

In Windows NT, the transition reaches KiSystemCall64, which vectors through the System Service Descriptor Table (SSDT). Arguments follow Microsoft x64 ABI (RCX, RDX, R8, R9, plus 32-byte shadow space on the stack). Windows enforces strict Structured Exception Handling (SEH) and Object Manager handle validation.
3.3 The Process Spawning Divergence: fork() vs CreateProcess()
The most radical architectural divergence between Linux and Windows occurs in process creation:

• Linux fork(): Relies on Copy-On-Write (COW). The kernel duplicates the parent's page tables and marks all pages read-only. Physical memory is NOT copied during fork(). Only when a process writes to a page does the CPU trigger a minor page fault, causing the kernel to allocate a new physical page frame. Hence, fork() executes in just 150 to 300 microseconds.

• Windows CreateProcess(): Windows lacks a native fork() primitive. CreateProcess creates a new executive process object (EPROCESS), sets up the Process Environment Block (PEB), opens and parses the Portable Executable (PE) headers from disk, maps imports, allocates the primary thread (ETHREAD), and initializes core DLLs (ntdll.dll, kernel32.dll). This heavyweight lifecycle requires over 3,000 microseconds (~10 to 20 times slower than Linux).

Microbenchmarks were conducted using high-resolution hardware timers (QueryPerformanceCounter on Windows and clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC) on Linux) over 2,000 to 10,000 iterations per system call. CPU times and memory working sets were collected via GetProcessTimes/GetProcessMemoryInfo and getrusage.
The discrete linear Kalman Filter estimates the true physical state of a kinematic system tracking position (p) and velocity (v) under process acceleration noise (q) and measurement noise (r).

State Prediction: x_hat_k(-) = F * x_hat_{k-1} + B * u_k P_k(-) = F * P_{k-1} * F^T + Q
Measurement Correction: y_k = z_k - H * x_hat_k(-) S_k = H * P_k(-) * H^T + R K_k = P_k(-) * H^T * S_k^(-1) x_hat_k = x_hat_k(-) + K_k * y_k P_k = (I - K_k * H) * P_k(-)
Rather than using standard C++ iostreams or thread pools, our architecture executes strictly through operating system system calls:
1. Sensor Ingestion: Master opens sensor CSV using open() / CreateFile() and buffers raw data using read() / ReadFile().
2. Shared Memory Allocation: Master maps an anonymous shared memory arena via mmap(MAP_SHARED | MAP_ANONYMOUS) on Linux or CreateFileMapping(INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE) + MapViewOfFile() on Windows.
3. Worker Forking: Master partitions the N dataset points across W worker processes using fork() on Linux or CreateProcess() on Windows.
4. IPC Pipe Coordination: Work assignments are dispatched across anonymous pipes (pipe() / CreatePipe()). Workers compute the Kalman estimates directly in the shared memory array.

5. Synchronization & Persistence: Master waits for all worker PIDs/Handles via waitpid() / WaitForSingleObject(), collects status structs from pipes, and persists the filtered trajectory to disk via write() / WriteFile().
6. Comparative Performance Evaluation & Amdahl's Law Analysis
The table below reports the empirical performance breakdown on a dataset of 200,000 sensor measurements comparing single-process execution against a 4-worker multi-process architecture on Windows NT.

Disk formatting + WriteFile flushing to disk
Process creation overhead dominates scalar computation

1. Amdahl's Law and I/O Dominance: Over 97% of the total execution time is spent in raw text serialization and disk I/O (CreateFile, WriteFile). The actual floating-point Kalman filtering arithmetic is computationally lightweight, requiring only 3.78 milliseconds for 200,000 points.

2. The Process Creation Overhead Penalty: In Windows NT, creating 4 child processes consumes approximately 4 x 3.26 ms = 13.04 ms, plus inter-process pipe communication latency. Because sequential computation is faster than process initialization, short-lived child processes are inefficient for fine-grained scalar math on Windows.

3. Architectural Recommendation: For CPU-bound tasks with lightweight compute per sample on Windows, multi-threading (CreateThread) or persistent worker pools should be utilized to avoid the heavy PE loader penalty. On Linux, fork() remains highly effective for fine-grained tasks due to lightweight Copy-On-Write cloning.

1. System Calls Are Not Simple Functions: A system call involves hardware privilege boundary switching, processor stack swaps, pipeline flushes, and kernel dispatch tables. High-performance software must minimize unnecessary crossings.

2. Paradigm Comparison: Linux POSIX emphasizes simple, orthogonal abstractions (fork, pipe, mmap), whereas Windows NT provides rich, declarative, object-oriented executive services (DACLs, handles, security descriptors) at the cost of higher invocation latency.

3. Systems Engineering Takeaway: Application performance is fundamentally dictated by operating system design choices. Systems programmers must tailor their concurrency and I/O models to the underlying OS architecture.
